theme: Evening and morning prayer, trust amid enemies
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 4 and Psalm 5. These are an evening prayer and a morning prayer, and they belong together. Notice the way each begins and how each ends with peace and protection.
settingTheScene: Psalm 4 is traditionally read as an evening prayer, and Psalm 5 as a morning prayer. Both are attributed to David and both appear in the early part of the Psalter. They come directly after Psalm 3, so the first five psalms of David form a rhythm of day and night: morning in Psalm 3, evening in Psalm 4, and morning in Psalm 5. David teaches us to pray at the edges of the day.
observation: “Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress” (4:1).
“But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him” (4:3).
“Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent” (4:4).
“There are many who say, Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!” (4:6).
“You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound” (4:7).
“In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (4:8).
“O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch” (5:3).
“But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you” (5:7).
interpretation:
Psalm 4 is a prayer to be said before going to sleep. David is troubled, but he does not simply complain. He recalls that God has given him relief before. He tells his opponents to “ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent.” The advice is good for anyone: before sleep, let your anger settle, and do not let it turn into sin. “Be angry, and do not sin” is one of the best pieces of advice in the Bible.

The psalm sets two kinds of happiness side by side. Many people say, “Who will show us some good?” They look for happiness in grain and wine, in material abundance. David asks for something different: “Lift up the light of your face upon us.” It is the blessing of Numbers 6, which you read in the last unit. And he says that God has put more joy in his heart than their abundance gives them. Joy that comes from God’s face is deeper than joy that comes from prosperity.

The last verse is among the most restful in the Psalter. “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.” The “alone” is important. Safety is not from locks or armies, but from the LORD.

Psalm 5 turns to the morning. David begins his day with prayer: “In the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.” The word “watch” suggests eager expectation. He lays out his prayer as a priest lays out the sacrifice, and then he looks to see how God will answer.

The psalm contrasts the wicked, whom God hates, with the righteous, who come into his house through his steadfast love. David enters by grace: “through the abundance of your steadfast love.” Our access to God does not rest on our goodness. He asks God to lead him in the way and make it straight. The psalm ends with the promise that God will bless the righteous and cover them “as with a shield.”
connection: Jesus began his days in prayer (Mark 1:35), and he withdrew to pray at night (Luke 6:12). Paul quotes Psalm 4:4 in Ephesians 4:26: “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” Paul also says, “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts” (Philippians 4:7). Psalm 5:9 is quoted in Romans 3:13 as a description of human sinfulness.
application:
Make a point of praying at the beginning and end of your day, even briefly.

Before bed tonight, let go of any anger you are holding. Do not let the sun go down on it.

Prepare your morning prayer as a sacrifice, and then watch to see how God answers.
prayerPrompts: Pray an evening prayer: give God today and what is unfinished.
Ask him to put more joy in your heart than abundance can.
Thank him that he alone makes you dwell in safety.
